questions.scenario: A clinic proposes storing patients, appointments and invoices in separate spreadsheets. Staff often overwrite another user’s changes. The team proposes a DBMS.

options.text: Receptionists need a duplicate patient table in order to see fewer patient columns.
options.why: A restricted view can expose fewer columns without duplicating patient records.

options.text: Access controls can give receptionists a narrower view than clinicians.
options.why: Views and permissions can restrict exposed data.

options.text: Keeping a continuously updated replica is enough to recover yesterday’s data after an accidental deletion, even without retained history.
options.why: The accidental deletion can propagate to the replica; retained backups or history are needed for an earlier state.

options.text: Database design must still identify patient and appointment identities.
options.why: A DBMS does not discover the correct business model automatically.

options.text: Concurrency control can reduce overwrite risk, but application transactions must use it appropriately.
options.why: A DBMS provides coordination facilities; simply moving data does not prove every workflow uses them correctly.

questions.explanation: Separate facilities the DBMS provides from policies and transactions the team must still design. A replica is not automatically a recoverable history.

questions.scenario: A library moves table storage from one disk layout to another. Its table definitions and application queries remain unchanged. Later it adds a column while keeping an existing user view unchanged.

options.text: Preserving the view after adding a column can illustrate logical independence.
options.why: The user interface can remain stable despite a conceptual schema extension.

options.text: Preserving one existing view proves that an application querying the new column directly will also need no change.
options.why: Independence of one interface does not establish independence for every application interface.

options.text: The user view and physical storage are different abstraction levels.
options.why: External and internal representations serve different concerns.

options.text: The disk change illustrates physical data independence.
options.why: Storage changed without a logical interface change.

options.text: Adding the new table column changes the logical schema even though the old user view stays stable.
options.why: A conceptual schema extension can be hidden behind a stable external view.

questions.explanation: Track which abstraction level changed and which interface remained stable. Stability of one view is not a guarantee about every application.

questions.scenario: A university team records that each course has one coordinator, draws an ER model, converts it to tables, then chooses indexes.
questions.prompt: Which reviews identify the appropriate work?

options.text: A correct ER diagram guarantees that every later relational mapping is free of redundancy, so refinement can be skipped.
options.why: The mapping still needs refinement; a sound conceptual model does not certify every implementation choice.

options.text: Performance and access-control requirements should first be collected after physical indexes have been selected.
options.why: Requirements analysis identifies performance and security constraints before later design choices are evaluated.

options.text: Confirm the coordinator rule during requirements analysis.
options.why: The rule should be established with stakeholders before implementing it.

options.text: Choose disk indexes as part of conceptual ER modelling.
options.why: Indexes are physical design choices.

options.text: Mapping the ER model to relational tables is logical design.
options.why: Logical design selects the database-model representation.

questions.explanation: Requirements constrain all later design decisions. Logical mapping, refinement, physical indexing and access design solve different problems.

questions.scenario: A small team needs a hosted reservation database, has little operations staff, and must meet a specified backup retention policy. A vendor offers managed hosting.

options.text: Evaluate network latency and availability against reservation needs.
options.why: Remote access adds network and service dependencies.

options.text: Check whether the service actually meets the retention requirement.
options.why: Managed does not automatically mean every retention policy is satisfied.

options.text: If the provider manages database patches, the application team no longer needs to decide who may read reservation details.
options.why: Operational maintenance does not decide business authorization rules.

options.text: Compare operating effort and total cost, not only disk price.
options.why: Management effort is part of the hosting decision.

options.text: A managed cloud service can host a relational database; cloud hosting does not require a NoSQL model.
options.why: Hosting location and management model are distinct from the data model; the lecture lists relational cloud services.

questions.explanation: Choose hosting against the actual retention, latency, management and cost needs; neither location nor managed maintenance decides the data model or business permissions.

questions.scenario: A telemetry service stores a million readings per hour but performs only simple arithmetic on each reading. A developer reads column types from the catalog. The DBA saves backups and the service has a two-minute recovery requirement.

options.text: Column definitions in the catalog are metadata.
options.why: They describe the structure and types of application data.

options.text: The service cannot be data-intensive because each calculation is simple.
options.why: Data-intensive workloads can be dominated by data volume, retrieval and storage rather than complex calculations.

options.text: The large reading stream makes storage throughput, retrieval and growth relevant design concerns.
options.why: The workload must reliably handle large and growing volumes of data.

options.text: Successful creation of a backup file alone proves the two-minute recovery requirement is met.
options.why: Recovery time depends on restoring and making the service usable; that must be evaluated separately.

options.text: Staff recovery procedures are outside the database system environment because they are not executable SQL.
options.why: The database system environment includes people and procedures, as well as hardware, software and data.

questions.explanation: Data-intensive does not mean computation-intensive. High data volume and modest arithmetic can still demand careful storage and recovery engineering.

questions.scenario: A shop creates Product(pid int PRIMARY KEY, price decimal(8,2) NULL CHECK(price>=0)). No other constraints or triggers exist.

options.text: A previously unused pid with price -1.
options.why: The CHECK evaluates FALSE.

options.text: A previously unused pid with price 0.
options.why: Zero satisfies price>=0.

options.text: An already existing pid with a different valid price.
options.why: The primary key must remain unique.

options.text: A NULL pid with a valid price.
options.why: Primary-key columns cannot be NULL.

options.text: A previously unused pid with price NULL.
options.why: The price comparison is UNKNOWN, which CHECK does not reject; price is nullable.

questions.explanation: A primary key rejects NULL and duplicates. A nullable price with CHECK(price>=0) rejects negative values, but UNKNOWN does not fail the CHECK.
questions.source: Lecture 02, slides 6–7; SQL Server CHECK/NULL semantics.

questions.scenario: A developer wants an enrolment identified by the pair (sid,cid), with sid referencing Student and cid referencing Course.

options.text: An enabled FK may reference a parent table that will only be created later in the same batch.
options.why: The referenced parent must exist when the FK is established; create it first or add the FK later.

options.text: Use one FK for sid and a separate FK for cid.
options.why: The columns reference two different parent keys.

options.text: A composite primary key makes sid alone unique.
options.why: Only the complete pair must be unique.

options.text: Use one table-level PRIMARY KEY(sid,cid).
options.why: A composite key is expressed as one constraint over both columns.

options.text: Declare sid PRIMARY KEY and cid PRIMARY KEY as two independent primary keys.
options.why: A table has one primary-key constraint; these declarations do not create the intended pair key.

questions.explanation: The identity is one pair, not two independent unique columns. Referenced objects must exist when enabled references are created.

questions.scenario: Dept has rows 10 and 20. Employee(eid PK,did NULL FK→Dept.did ON DELETE SET NULL) contains (1,10),(2,10),(3,20).
questions.prompt: After deleting Dept 10, which statements hold?

options.text: Dept 20 remains.
options.why: Only department 10 was deleted.

options.text: The action would work unchanged if did were NOT NULL.
options.why: SET NULL requires nullable referencing columns.

options.text: Employees 1 and 2 remain.
options.why: SET NULL changes the reference instead of deleting child rows.

options.text: Employees 1 and 2 have NULL did.
options.why: That is the specified referential action.

options.text: If ON DELETE CASCADE were used instead, employees 1 and 2 would be deleted with Dept 10.
options.why: CASCADE removes referencing child rows rather than setting their references to NULL.

questions.explanation: Trace the specified referential action separately from the parent deletion. SET NULL and CASCADE produce different child outcomes.

questions.scenario: Reading(rid PK,value NULL) contains (1,5),(2,NULL),(3,0).

options.text: WHERE value=5 OR value IS NULL returns rid 1 and rid 2.
options.why: Each of those rows satisfies one side of the disjunction.

options.text: WHERE value<>5 returns only rid 3.
options.why: NULL<>5 is UNKNOWN, not TRUE.

options.text: WHERE value=5 OR value<>5 returns only rid 1 and rid 3.
options.why: For NULL both comparisons are UNKNOWN, so their OR is still UNKNOWN and rid 2 is excluded.

options.text: WHERE value IS NULL returns rid 2.
options.why: IS NULL directly tests missing values.

options.text: WHERE NOT(value=5) returns rid 2 and rid 3.
options.why: NOT UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN, so rid 2 is excluded.

questions.explanation: SQL predicates must be TRUE to survive WHERE. UNKNOWN is not FALSE, and negation does not turn UNKNOWN into TRUE.

questions.scenario: Offer(id,region,price) contains (1,East,150),(2,West,80),(3,West,150),(4,North,50).
questions.prompt: Which claims about the following filter are correct?
questions.code: WHERE region='East' OR region='West' AND price<100

options.text: Offer 1 is selected.
options.why: AND binds before OR, so every East row satisfies the left branch.

options.text: Offer 2 would be excluded unless parentheses were added around the region comparisons.
options.why: The original predicate already accepts West rows whose price is below 100.

options.text: Offer 3 is selected.
options.why: It fails the price requirement on the West branch.

options.text: Adding parentheses around the two region tests would remove offer 1.
options.why: Then the price condition would also apply to East.

options.text: Offer 4 is selected because its price is below 100.
options.why: It satisfies neither region branch.

questions.explanation: Evaluate AND before OR. The price restriction belongs to the West branch until parentheses change the expression.

questions.scenario: Payment(pid,amount decimal(8,2) NULL) has rows (1,100),(2,NULL),(3,200),(4,100).

options.text: COUNT(amount) = 3.
options.why: The NULL amount is ignored.

options.text: AVG(amount) = 100.
options.why: The average is 400/3, not 400/4.

options.text: SUM(amount) = 400.
options.why: The three known amounts sum to 400.

options.text: COUNT(DISTINCT amount) = 3.
options.why: Only two distinct non-NULL amounts exist: 100 and 200.

options.text: COUNT(*) = 4.
options.why: All rows are counted.

questions.explanation: Count rows separately from known values and distinct known values. AVG uses three non-NULL decimal values here.

questions.scenario: Sale(agent,amount) contains (A,40),(A,80),(B,100),(B,20). A manager wants agents whose total sales exceed 110, counting all their sales.
questions.prompt: Which query fragments or result claims correctly support that request?

options.text: SELECT agent,SUM(amount) with the correct grouping.
options.why: The total per agent is the requested measure.

options.text: HAVING amount>110 without grouping or aggregation of amount.
options.why: The individual amount is not a valid group-level expression here.

options.text: DISTINCT is required to keep both agents because their aggregate totals are equal.
options.why: The rows have different agent values; GROUP BY already produces one row per agent, regardless of equal totals.

options.text: GROUP BY agent HAVING SUM(amount)>110.
options.why: Both A and B have totals of 120.

options.text: WHERE amount>110 GROUP BY agent.
options.why: Filtering individual rows removes every row before totals are formed.

questions.explanation: WHERE acts on individual sales before grouping; HAVING acts on each agent’s total after grouping. Both totals are 120.

questions.scenario: Member has IDs 1,2,3. Loan(lid PK,mid FK) contains (10,1),(11,1),(12,2).
questions.prompt: For the query below, which claims are true?

options.text: The join produces four rows before grouping.
options.why: Two for member 1, one for member 2, one unmatched row for member 3.

options.text: After changing to INNER JOIN, COUNT(*) and COUNT(l.lid) agree for every remaining member group.
options.why: Every retained joined row has a non-NULL matching loan primary key.

options.text: Member 1 has n=2.
options.why: Two child rows match.

options.text: Member 3 has n=0.
options.why: COUNT(l.lid) ignores the NULL-extended child value.

options.text: Replacing COUNT(l.lid) with COUNT(*) still gives member 3 zero.
options.why: The preserved row itself is counted by COUNT(*).

questions.explanation: Expand the join before counting: member 1 has two rows, member 2 one, and member 3 one NULL-extended row.

questions.scenario: Member has IDs 1,2,3. Loan(lid,mid,state) contains (10,1,Open),(11,2,Closed). The report must include every member and count only open loans.
questions.prompt: Which changes or conclusions are valid?

options.text: WHERE l.state='Open' OR l.lid IS NULL always fixes the problem.
options.why: Member 2 has a matched Closed loan, so it gets no NULL-extended row and is removed.

options.text: Put l.state='Open' in the LEFT JOIN ON condition.
options.why: The match is restricted while unmatched parents remain.

options.text: Put l.state='Open' only in WHERE after the LEFT JOIN.
options.why: This removes members whose joined state is Closed or NULL.

options.text: With the open-loan predicate in ON, use COUNT(l.lid), grouped by member ID.
options.why: After restricting matches to open loans, COUNT of the child key counts qualifying children and gives zero for missing matches.

options.text: With the correct ON filter, members 2 and 3 both receive zero.
options.why: Neither has a qualifying open loan.

questions.explanation: A Closed child is a real match before a WHERE filter. Filtering matches in ON is what creates a preserved zero-open-loan group for that member.

questions.scenario: One customer has two orders with distinct non-NULL orderIDs and three independent support tickets with distinct ticketIDs. A query joins Customer to Orders and Ticket using customer ID, with no other restrictions.

options.text: The customer contributes six joined rows.
options.why: Each of the two orders pairs with each of three tickets.

options.text: COUNT(orderID) over that join is two.
options.why: Each order appears three times, producing six counted values.

options.text: COUNT(DISTINCT orderID) gives two for this customer.
options.why: Distinct removes the repeated order IDs.

options.text: Pre-aggregating orders and tickets separately can prevent inflated counts.
options.why: One summary row per customer avoids the two-by-three multiplication.

options.text: SUM(DISTINCT orderAmount) is always a safe repair for inflated revenue.
options.why: Two genuinely different orders may have the same amount and would be wrongly merged.

questions.explanation: Two independent one-to-many joins produce a two-by-three product. Removing duplicate values is not the same as counting distinct business objects.

questions.scenario: Employee(eid,did) and Dept(did,name) are joined on matching department ID. The intended result excludes employees without a matching department.
questions.prompt: Which implementations or claims are valid?

options.text: FROM Employee e, Dept d WHERE e.did=d.did.
options.why: The predicate filters the Cartesian product to matching pairs.

options.text: FROM Employee e, Dept d with no predicate gives the same result in every database.
options.why: It returns every pair, not only matching pairs.

options.text: Replacing INNER JOIN with LEFT JOIN, without a later filter, still guarantees unmatched employees are excluded.
options.why: LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched employees, contrary to the intended report.

options.text: An inner join always produces one row per employee regardless of the right table.
options.why: Multiplicity depends on matching rows and constraints.

options.text: FROM Employee e JOIN Dept d ON e.did=d.did.
options.why: This is an explicit inner join.

questions.explanation: Implicit and explicit inner joins express the same matching-pair condition. A left join changes unmatched-row preservation.

questions.scenario: Book has IDs 10,20. Loan(lid,bid) contains only (1,10). A report uses Loan RIGHT JOIN Book ON Loan.bid=Book.bid.

options.text: Swapping table order to Book LEFT JOIN Loan with the same ON condition preserves the same book/loan pairings.
options.why: Both formulations preserve Book; compare the same explicitly selected columns rather than SELECT * column order.

options.text: Book 10 appears with loan ID 1.
options.why: The matching pair is retained.

options.text: For the unmatched book 20, Book.bid remains 20 while Loan.bid is NULL in the result.
options.why: Only the missing Loan-side columns are NULL-extended; the preserved Book row retains its own values.

options.text: Book 20 appears with a NULL loan ID.
options.why: The right table is preserved.

options.text: Book 20 is removed because it has no loan.
options.why: That would be inner-join behaviour.

questions.explanation: The preserved Book side keeps its values, while missing Loan-side values become NULL. This changes query results, not stored records.

questions.scenario: Employee IDs are 1,2,3. Assignment.ownerID contains 1 and NULL.
questions.prompt: Which conclusions follow under SQL NULL rules?

options.text: Filtering NULL out of the NOT IN subquery makes employees 2 and 3 pass.
options.why: The remaining set contains only 1.

options.text: NULL in the subquery matches every employee ID.
options.why: NULL comparisons are unknown, not universal matches.

options.text: eid IN (SELECT ownerID FROM Assignment) returns employee 1.
options.why: The comparison finds a true match for 1.

options.text: eid NOT IN (SELECT ownerID FROM Assignment) returns employees 2 and 3.
options.why: The NULL causes UNKNOWN for those nonmatching IDs.

options.text: A correlated NOT EXISTS test can find employees 2 and 3.
options.why: Neither has an equal ownerID row; NULL does not match their IDs.

questions.explanation: A NULL inside NOT IN can make every nonmatching comparison UNKNOWN. A properly correlated NOT EXISTS asks whether an equal row exists.
questions.source: Lecture 02, slide 12; Lab 08 nested queries; SQL NULL semantics.

questions.scenario: Book prices are 100,200,200. A student writes price=(SELECT price FROM Book) in a WHERE clause.

options.text: A zero-row scalar subquery normally behaves as the number zero.
options.why: It yields NULL, not numeric zero.

options.text: The scalar subquery fails because it returns more than one row.
options.why: A scalar expression cannot accept these three rows.

options.text: The repeated 200 automatically collapses the result to one row.
options.why: SQL does not remove duplicate rows implicitly, and even DISTINCT gives 100 and 200.

options.text: Replacing the subquery with SELECT MAX(price) returns the two highest-priced books.
options.why: MAX returns the single scalar 200.

options.text: Using price IN (SELECT price FROM Book) accepts all three books here.
options.why: Each price belongs to that set.

questions.explanation: A scalar subquery permits at most one row. An aggregate can produce one scalar; IN deliberately accepts a multiple-row result.

questions.scenario: A comparison subquery returns the non-NULL values 40 and 70. A product price is 60.

options.text: 60 > ANY(subquery) is true.
options.why: 60 exceeds at least one value: 40.

options.text: Replacing ANY with SOME leaves these comparisons unchanged.
options.why: SOME and ANY are SQL synonyms.

options.text: 60 < ANY(subquery) is true.
options.why: 60 is below 70.

options.text: For an empty subquery, >ALL is true.
options.why: Universal comparison over an empty set is true.

options.text: For an empty subquery, >ANY is true.
options.why: There is no witness satisfying the comparison.

questions.explanation: ANY/SOME needs a true witness; ALL needs no counterexample. This explains both the 40/70 comparisons and the empty-set results.

questions.scenario: Book contains (1,SQL,100),(2,SQL,100),(3,ER,120), with columns bid,title,price.

options.text: SELECT DISTINCT bid,title,price returns two rows.
options.why: The different primary keys keep all three projected tuples distinct.

options.text: ORDER BY price DESC,bid ASC places bid 3 first.
options.why: 120 is the highest price.

options.text: TOP(1) without ORDER BY guarantees bid 3.
options.why: No deterministic ordering is specified.

options.text: Adding bid to the ORDER BY makes the tied 100-price rows ordered deterministically.
options.why: The unique bid breaks the tie.

options.text: SELECT DISTINCT title,price returns two rows.
options.why: The first two rows become one identical projected pair.

questions.explanation: DISTINCT applies to the whole projected tuple. Stable TOP selection needs ordering, and tied prices need a unique tie-breaker.
questions.source: Lecture 02, slides 15, 17; SQL Server TOP application.

questions.scenario: Code values are AB12, AB123, XB12 and AB1. Numeric scores are checked independently with BETWEEN 50 AND 80.

options.text: LIKE 'AB%' excludes AB1.
options.why: Percent may match any suffix length, including one character.

options.text: BETWEEN 50 AND 80 includes both boundary scores.
options.why: BETWEEN is inclusive.

options.text: BETWEEN 50 AND 80 includes a NULL score.
options.why: The comparisons are UNKNOWN for NULL.

options.text: LIKE 'AB__' matches AB12 but not AB123.
options.why: Two underscores require exactly two following characters.

options.text: LIKE '%B12' matches AB12 and XB12.
options.why: The percent accepts either prefix.

questions.explanation: Match the whole code against the pattern. Percent matches any-length suffix, underscore one character, and BETWEEN includes both numeric endpoints.

questions.scenario: A shop has three Product rows. The developer runs UPDATE Product SET price=price*1.1 with no WHERE, then DELETE FROM Product WHERE pid=999, where no such ID exists.

options.text: DROP TABLE Product would remove rows but retain the empty table definition for later INSERT statements.
options.why: DROP removes the table object; DELETE removes rows while retaining the table.

options.text: The UPDATE automatically creates an audit history table.
options.why: No such trigger or auditing setup was specified.

options.text: The UPDATE targets every product row.
options.why: No WHERE limits its target set.

options.text: The DELETE removes all three rows because 999 is absent.
options.why: A nonmatching predicate deletes zero rows.

options.text: The table definition remains after the DELETE.
options.why: DELETE removes qualifying rows, not the table object.

questions.explanation: Separate row-changing statements from object-changing statements. An absent match deletes nothing; missing WHERE targets all rows.

questions.scenario: A report filters all Payment rows out before aggregating and does not use GROUP BY.

options.text: The ungrouped aggregate query necessarily returns no result row.
options.why: It returns one aggregate row even with no input rows.

options.text: COUNT(*) returns zero.
options.why: No input rows are counted.

options.text: SUM(amount) returns NULL.
options.why: SUM has no non-NULL input values.

options.text: COALESCE(SUM(amount),0) returns zero.
options.why: COALESCE substitutes the requested default.

options.text: MIN(amount) returns NULL.
options.why: There is no input value from which to compute a minimum.

questions.explanation: An ungrouped aggregate returns one summary row even with empty input. COUNT has result zero; SUM/MIN/AVG have NULL unless replaced.

questions.scenario: Customer IDs are 1,2. Order(oid,cid,total) contains (10,1,50),(11,1,50). The goal is every customer with total order value, using zero where no order exists.

options.text: Use LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY customer ID, and COALESCE(SUM(o.total),0).
options.why: That preserves customer 2 and replaces its NULL sum with zero.

options.text: Use SUM(DISTINCT o.total) to ensure customer 1 receives 100.
options.why: DISTINCT collapses the two equal amounts and gives 50.

options.text: Expect customer 1 to receive 100.
options.why: Two different orders each contribute 50.

options.text: Expect customer 2 to receive 0 after COALESCE.
options.why: Its preserved group has no non-NULL order value.

options.text: Put o.total>0 in WHERE and still guarantee every customer appears.
options.why: The NULL-extended row for customer 2 fails that predicate.

questions.explanation: Preserve customers first, aggregate each customer’s real orders, then substitute zero for the missing total. Equal order values are still separate revenue.
